questions.title: Define Macro Purpose
questions.description: What does the directive #define PI 3.14 do in a C program?
questions.Option1: Defines PI as a symbolic constant whose occurrences are replaced by 3.14
questions.Option2: Declares a typed variable PI of type double initialized to 3.14
questions.Option3: Allocates 3.14 bytes of memory at the symbol PI
questions.Option4: Imports the constant PI from a math library

questions.title: Include Directive Action
questions.description: What does #include <stdio.h> do at preprocessing time?
questions.Option1: Replaces the directive with the contents of the standard stdio.h header file
questions.Option3: Links the standard library at runtime

questions.title: Ifdef Check Meaning
questions.description: What does the directive #ifdef DEBUG check during preprocessing?
questions.Option1: Whether DEBUG is defined as a macro (regardless of its value)
questions.Option2: Whether DEBUG is a typed integer variable
questions.Option4: Whether DEBUG was declared in a header file

questions.title: Pragma Directive Nature
questions.description: What is the role of the #pragma directive in C?
questions.Option1: It provides implementation-specific directives to the compiler (e.g. controlling alignment or warnings)
questions.Option2: It defines a new preprocessor macro
questions.Option4: It is required at the start of every C file

questions.title: Macro vs Const Variable
questions.description: What is a key difference between #define PI 3.14 and const double PI = 3.14;?
questions.Option1: Macros are pure text substitutions performed by the preprocessor; const variables are typed and have an address in memory
questions.Option2: const variables cannot be used in expressions; macros cannot
questions.Option3: Macros take priority over const variables at link time
questions.Option4: There is no difference between them

questions.title: Angle Brackets vs Quotes
questions.description: What is the difference between #include <header.h> and #include "header.h"?
questions.Option1: <> searches the system include paths; "" searches the current source directory first, then falls back to system paths
questions.Option2: "" searches only the system paths; <> searches the local directory
questions.Option3: Both forms are exactly identical in behavior
questions.Option4: <> is for C++ only; "" is for C only

questions.title: Ifndef Inverse Check

questions.Option1: Whether HEADER_GUARD is NOT currently defined as a macro
questions.Option2: Whether HEADER_GUARD is defined as a macro
